extracted.intended_audience: general readers, legislative staff, regulatory lawyers, policy students, and journalists interested in federal rulemaking and Congressional oversight
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive requirements under the Congressional Review Act (CRA) for Congress, GAO, and agencies when reviewing, submitting, and disapproving federal agency rules, including timing, required submissions, and Senate/House parliamentary mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency report submission requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a rule can take effect, the agency promulgating the rule must submit a report (containing the rule, a concise general statement of the rule, and the rule’s proposed effective date) to each House of Congress and the Comptroller General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each House then sends copies of the report to the Chairs and Ranking Members of committees with jurisdiction and prints notices of the report in the Congressional Record as executive communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60-session-day window for disapproval and special procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has a window of time lasting 60 session days to disapprove of any given rule by simple-majority vote; the Act makes special parliamentary procedures available for that 60-day period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These special, fast-track Senate procedures make it easier to pass a joint resolution of disapproval (e.g., a qualifying joint resolution cannot be filibustered). The special procedures cease after 60 session days in the Senate, while the House can act anytime during the 2-year Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting date calculation for the 60-day period
rubrics_metrics.description: The starting date for the 60-session-day period is determined by: the House focusing on the date it received the report, the Senate focusing on the date the notice is published in the Congressional Record and the report is referred to committee; the later of those dates or the date the rule is published in the Federal Register becomes the starting date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency fails to publish the rule in the Federal Register and GAO determines it is nonetheless a rule, then the starting date is the date on which a Senator publishes the GAO decision in the Congressional Record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing restrictions on introducing joint resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for expedited consideration in the Senate, a joint resolution of disapproval may not be introduced before the starting date, and a joint resolution introduced after the 60-day period ends does not qualify for the Act's special procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that 21 or more days after the starting date, a Senator can submit the joint resolution and discharge it immediately, even before the committee has any opportunity to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required form/text of a joint resolution of disapproval
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint resolution of disapproval must use only the words, “That Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the ____ relating to ____, and such rule shall have no force or effect,” where blanks are filled with the agency and title of the rule and either the Federal Register citation or the Congressional Record citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resolution must identify the rule and include the appropriate citation (Federal Register if published there, Congressional Record citation if GAO determined it to be a rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate discharge petition procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning 21 calendar days after the starting date, Senators can discharge the resolution with a petition signed by 30 Senators (if the committee to which a joint resolution was referred has not already reported the resolution or an identical resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If discharged, the joint resolution is placed on the calendar; note the timing requirement (21 days) and the 30-Senator signature threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to proceed is nondebatable and unamendable
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the joint resolution has been placed on the calendar, any Senator can make a nondebatable, unamendable motion to proceed to the joint resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Senator cannot make such a motion if the Senate has invoked cloture, if another privileged motion to proceed is pending, or if the Senate is in executive session; it is in order to proceed while a motion to proceed to a non-privileged matter is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on debate in the Senate (ten-hour rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act limits debate on the joint resolution (and on all motions and appeals) to 10 hours, equally divided between those favoring and those opposing the resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limit ensures that a simple majority vote will decide the matter. Any Senator can make a nondebatable motion to further limit debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No amendments or motions to recommit allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The law does not allow amendments or motions to recommit to a joint resolution of disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By precedent, Senators may raise points of order; the Senate decides appeals from decisions of the Presiding Officer without debate. Immediately after conclusion of debate (and a single quorum call if requested), the Senate votes on final passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: GAO role in determining what is a 'rule'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) evaluates whether administrative actions constitute 'rules' under the CRA and issues legal decisions on that question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency does not submit an action as a rule and GAO then determines it is a rule, the Senate Parliamentarian gives effect to GAO's position. Historically, when GAO decided an action was not a rule, the Senate did not consider disapproval (until recent precedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: GAO reporting duty for major rules (15-day report)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires the Comptroller General (GAO) to provide a report on each major rule to the committees of jurisdiction in each House of Congress by the end of 15 calendar days after the submission or publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GAO report must include an assessment of the agency’s compliance with procedural steps required and any other relevant information or requirements under other Acts or Executive orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency cooperation with the Comptroller General
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies shall cooperate with the Comptroller General by providing information relevant to the Comptroller General’s report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuant to statutory authorization, GAO has regularly evaluated whether administrative actions constitute 'rules' and agencies are statutorily required to provide relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a successful CRA disapproval on reissuing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a rule is repealed under the CRA, the Act prohibits the reissuing of the rule in substantially the same form or the issuing of a new rule that is substantially the same unless the reissued or new rule is specifically authorized by a law enacted after the date of the joint resolution disapproving the original rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bar on reissuance is a substantive effect of an enacted CRA resolution of disapproval and can block agencies from simply republishing the same regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting of the 60-day period with respect to adjournments
rubrics_metrics.description: The 60-day period counts calendar days, 'excluding days either House of Congress is adjourned for more than 3 days during a session of Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress adjourns for the 2-year Congress within 60 days of session in the Senate or 60 legislative days in the House after Congress receives a rule, then the 60-day period for special procedures begins anew in the next Congress on the 15th day of session in the Senate and the 15th legislative day in the House (the 'lookback' process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lookback mechanism when Congress adjourns
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress adjourns within the relevant 60-day period, the 60-day period for special procedures restarts in the next Congress (beginning on the 15th day of session in the Senate and the 15th legislative day in the House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lookback process preserves the ability to use the CRA across a change in Congress or at the start of a new Presidency; a joint resolution still requires Presidential agreement or a veto override to become law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'major rule'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'major rule' is one that would likely (1) affect the economy by $100 million or more a year; (2) cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, industries, government, or regions; or (3) significantly affect competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S. businesses to compete with foreign competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO provides reports on major rules and these designations have implications for congressional review and GAO reporting duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate precedent and interplay with GAO determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When GAO has concluded an action is not a rule, historically the Senate did not pursue CRA disapproval; however, Senate action and rulings (e.g., Parliamentarian decisions, points of order, and floor votes) can create new precedents affecting whether expedited procedures apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include disputes over EPA waiver notices and Senate votes to sustain points of order creating precedents about whether matters submitted by agencies or determined by GAO are entitled to expedited procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that joint resolution identify citation source
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint resolution must include either the Federal Register citation (if the agency published the rule there) or the Congressional Record citation (if GAO determined it to be a rule and it was entered into the Record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the resolution unambiguously identifies the agency action being disapproved.
